conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported during these first weeks with your new baby.

Today I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, ten-question screen that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a snapshot that helps us see if you might benefit from extra support right now.

Everything we discuss is confidential. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause or stop. All I ask is that you answer as honestly as you can; there are no right or wrong responses.

I’ll read each question one at a time, and you can tell me which option best matches how you’ve felt. When we’re done I’ll add up the numbers and we can talk about what they mean and what next steps might help.

Ready? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I still laugh sometimes—like if my husband makes a joke or the baby does something silly—but it feels kind of forced. I’d say “not so much now,” maybe half-and-half with “definitely not.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d go with “not so much now.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’d say “rather less.” I still get a little excited if we’re planning a walk or someone’s coming to see the baby, but it’s nowhere near the happy buzz I used to feel before she was born.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Yeah... I do that sometimes. Like if the baby won’t settle, I’ll think maybe I missed her cues or didn’t swaddle her right. Nothing major, but it pops into my head. I’d say “yes, some of the time.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Mostly “no, not at all.” I do worry, but it’s always about the baby—her breathing, her feeding, her temperature. It’s not out-of-the-blue anxiety; there’s usually a reason, even if it’s small.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, that hasn’t happened—at least not for no reason. If I hear her cough funny or the monitor glitches, my heart races, but I know why. So “no, not at all.”
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes. A few nights a week when she won’t sleep and I’m bone-tired, I feel like I’m drowning. But I still manage to get through the day. I’ll circle “yes, sometimes.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Yeah, a couple of nights. I lie there thinking I’m doing everything wrong, and then I can’t drift off even when the baby’s quiet. I’d say “yes, most of the time.”
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had that feeling a few days this week—like a heavy blanket that settles in the afternoon. It lifts if someone visits or I get a decent nap, but it keeps coming back. I’d tick “yes, sometimes.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up once when I couldn’t get her to latch and the lactation consultant was running late, but I didn’t full-on cry. I’d go with “no, never.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No. That idea hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that over the past week laughter and excitement feel muted, you sometimes blame yourself when the baby fusses, and several afternoons a heavy, sad "blanket" settles in. Nights are the hardest: even when your daughter sleeps you lie awake thinking you are "doing everything wrong." These feelings come and go, yet you continue to meet her needs and cherish small moments of joy.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly acknowledges self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, matching the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent overwhelm ('drowning' when baby won't sleep) but still functioning, aligning with 'sometimes not coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "yes, most of the time" and describes multiple nights of sleep difficulty due to unhappiness, matching the highest-severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring sadness several days this week, consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places 12 in the 12-13 range indicating high likelihood of <med>perinatal depression</med>. Key items: Q7 (sleep disturbance secondary to unhappiness) scored 3; Q3,6,8 each scored 2, endorsing <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>, and frequent <sym>sad mood</sym>. While Q10 (self-harm) was 0 and Q9 (crying) 0, persistence of multiple neuro-vegetative and cognitive-affective symptoms for over two weeks aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No safety concerns today. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next week to discuss these results and consider treatment options
2. Continue EPDS re-screen every 2 weeks until scores drop below 9
3. Arrange practical support: partner or family member to cover one night feed so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Try brief daily mood boosters: 10-minute stroller walk outside, shower while listening to music, or text a friend-choose one per day
5. Access local resources: postpartum support group (virtual or in-person) and national hotline 1-833-943-5746 (Postpartum Support International)
6. If low mood worsens, sleep further deteriorates, or any thoughts of self-harm emerge, seek urgent evaluation same day
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit (PHQ-9/EPDS items)

Symptoms endorsed
- Diminished pleasure/laughter (“not so much now”; “rather less” enjoyment)
- Intermittent low mood (“sad or miserable” several afternoons/week)
- Sleep disturbance mood-related (“difficulty sleeping” most nights secondary to ruminating “doing everything wrong”)
- Self-blame/guilt (“yes, some of the time” when baby won’t settle)
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning sensation “sometimes” when infant won’t sleep

Symptoms denied
- Panic or anxiety without situational trigger; worries focus on infant safety
- Crying spells (only one episode of tearing up)
- Thoughts of self-harm (endorsed “No”)

Pattern
Mild-to-moderate affective symptoms emerging 2° to fatigue and maternal self-doubt; no safety concerns at present. Findings suggest possible subsyndromal postpartum depression; routine follow-up and continued monitoring recommended.
